paragraphs: Selective breeding (i.e. artificial selection) is the process by which humans use animal breeding and plant breeding to selectively develop desired traits
We’ve been doing it for longer than most people realize…
“Accidental” selective breeding of wheat began as early as 9000 BC in the Middle East
Farmers were able to collect and plant the seeds of one variety of wheat more easily than the other, thus “selecting for” this former strain without realizing it

paragraphs: Traits are determined by specific genes, or segments of DNA. Different variations of genes are known as alleles. In most cases, one allele is dominant over the other, influencing the way such genes are expressed…
The dominant allele (represented by capital letter) is always expressed when present
A recessive allele (represented by lowercase letter) is only expressed in the absence of the dominant allele.
The allele that encodes brown eyes (B), for example, is dominant over the recessive allele that encodes blue eyes (b).

paragraphs: This means that although we receive genes from both parents, our characteristics are NOT determined by the “blending” of our parents traits. It is determined by the dominant vs. recessive interaction of the alleles we receive.
Phenotype refers to the outward expression of traits. For example, having brown eyes or having blue eyes.
Genotype on the other hand refers to the combination of alleles an individual has for a given trait.
For example, your teacher’s genotype for eye color is ‘bb’. Since she only has recessive alleles, this means that her phenotype is ‘having blue eyes’
Note: A phenotype isn’t always a visible trait like color. It could be a behaviour or a physiological trait, such as ‘able to digest lactose’ or ‘not able to digest lactose.

paragraphs: The idea of dominant and recessive alleles was first described by Gregor Mendel…
He conducted test crosses with peas of different phenotypes and realized that for each trait, offspring displayed either the maternal or paternal phenotype rather than a blending of the two.

E.g. a true-breeding (i.e. homozygous) plant with purple flowers crossed with a true-breeding (i.e. homozygous) plant with white flowers always produced offspring with purple flowers, not light purple as previously suggested by the blending theory of inheritance
Thus, he concluded that purple flowers were dominant to white

List the genotypes of a black mouse and a brown mouse.
If a heterozygous black mouse is crossed with a brown mouse, what is the probability that their offspring will have black fur? Brown fur?
Possible genotypes for a black mouse: BB or Bb
Possible genotype of a brown mouse: bb
The probability of having black fur is 2/4 = 1/2  or 0.50.
The probability of having brown fur is  also 2/4 = 1/2  or 0.50.

paragraphs: If two heterozygous black mice are crossed, what will be the genotypic and phenotypic ratio of their offspring?

A 1:2:1 genotypic ratio and/or a 3:1 phenotypic ratio is highly indicative that we are dealing with a monohybrid cross, which is a cross between two organisms that are both heterozygous for a single trait.

paragraphs: Is it possible for a homozygous black mouse and a heterozygous black mouse to have ‘children’ that are brown? How about “grandchildren” that are brown?
No children will be brown, because each possible combination has at least one dominant black allele.
If two of the heterozygous children from the F1 generation reproduce, they will have a ¼ chance of having brown offspring. So yes!

paragraphs: Is it possible for a homozygous black mouse and a heterozygous black mouse to have ‘children’ that are brown? How about “grandchildren” that are brown?
If two of the heterozygous children from the F1 generation reproduce, they will have a ¼ chance of having brown offspring. So yes!

We just observed how recessive phenotypes can ‘skip’ generations. This is because they are being masked by the dominant allele, but they are still present and will show up if paired with another recessive allele.

paragraphs: We just observed how recessive phenotypes can ‘skip’ generations. This is because they are being masked by the dominant allele, but they are still present and will show up if paired with another recessive allele.

paragraphs: An individual with the dominant phenotype could be either homozygous (BB) or heterozygous (Bb). By performing a test cross, we can determine the true genotype of such individuals.
Cross the unknown individual (B?) with an individual who displays the recessive phenotype (bb) (because their genotype is known):
If the unknown was homozygous, all offspring will show dominant phenotype
If heterozygous, some (typically half) offspring will show recessive phenotype

paragraphs: If the unknown was homozygous, all offspring will show dominant phenotype
If heterozygous, some (typically half) offspring will show recessive phenotype

Note: This will typically require sufficient number of offspring so we can feel confident about which outcome we are observing. If the recessive phenotype is present, this is sufficient to conclude that the unknown must have been heterozygous. But we need a good number of offspring showing only the dominant phenotype to feel confident declaring the unknown homozygous, to rule out it occurring due to random chance.

View full lesson: http://ed.ted.com/lessons/how-mendel-s-pea-plants-helped-us-understand-genetics-hortensia-jimenez-diaz

Each father and mother pass down traits to their children, who inherit combinations of their dominant or recessive alleles. But how do we know so much about genetics today? Hortensia Jiménez Díaz explains how studying pea plants revealed why you may have blue eyes.

Lesson by Hortensia Jiménez Díaz, animation by Cinematic Sweden.

paragraphs: Because such crosses consistently yielded this 9:3:3:1 ratio, Mendel concluded that the segregation of alleles for one gene had no influence on the segregation of alleles for another gene…
This is known as Mendel’s Second Law, or the Law of Independent Assortment:
The two alleles for one gene segregate independently of alleles for other genes during gamete formation.

paragraphs: In tomatoes, red fruit is dominant to yellow fruit, and tall plants are dominant to short plants. A plant that is heterozygous for both traits is crossed with a plant that is heterozygous for the gene encoding height, and homozygous recessive for the gene encoding fruit colour.
What are the phenotypes & genotypes of the plants being crossed?
‘Red fruit is dominant to yellow’ so let’s use ‘R’ to represent red and ‘r’ to represent the yellow allele.
Similarly, if ‘tall is dominant to short’ let’s use ‘T’ to represent the tall allele and ‘t’ to represent the short allele.
So the parents phenotypes and genotypes are:
Plant that is heterozygous for both traits

shapes.name: Google Shape;680;p55
paragraphs: In tomatoes, red fruit is dominant to yellow fruit, and tall plants are dominant to short plants. A plant that is heterozygous for both traits is crossed with a plant that is heterozygous for the gene encoding height, and homozygous recessive for the gene encoding fruit colour.
What are the phenotypes & genotypes of the plants being crossed?

paragraphs: In tomatoes, red fruit is dominant to yellow fruit, and tall plants are dominant to short plants. A plant that is heterozygous for both traits is crossed with a plant that is heterozygous for the gene encoding height, and homozygous recessive for the gene encoding fruit colour.
Step 1 with a cross is to identify the genotypes of the parents. This we have already done in part a:

Step 2 is to identify the possible gametes and set up the Punnett Square. Not all two trait crosses will require a large 4x4 Punnett Square. Just identify the possible gametes and construct accordingly.
So parent 1 can make the RT, Rt, rT, and rt gametes, while parent 2 can only make rT and rt gametes.
There is no need to consider the other four combinations because they will be repeat and will not impact the ratio.

paragraphs: In summer squash, white fruit color (W) is dominant over yellow fruit color (w) and disk-shaped fruit (D) is dominant over sphere-shaped fruit (d). A plant that produces yellow, disk-shaped fruit is crossed with a plant that produces white, sphere-shaped fruit.
What are the potential genotypes of the plants being crossed?

We know that the parents display some of the dominant phenotypes, but we don’t know just yet whether they are homozygous dominant or heterozygous for those traits, since both cases would display the dominant phenotype. We can represent this unknown allele by the line:
b) Some of the offspring have yellow, sphere-shaped fruit. What does this tell us about the genotypes of the parents?
The genotype of these offspring with yellow, sphere-shaped fruit must be homozygous recessive for both traits, so wwdd. This is only possible, if BOTH parents had a copy of both w and d alleles.

paragraphs: In summer squash, white fruit color (W) is dominant over yellow fruit color (w) and disk-shaped fruit (D) is dominant over sphere-shaped fruit (d). A plant that produces yellow, disk-shaped fruit is crossed with a plant that produces white, sphere-shaped fruit.
c) If this parental cross produces 80 seeds, how many of those seeds would give rise to
Squash with yellow and sphere-shaped flowers?

shapes.description:
This video will show how to set up and solve everyone's favorite 16 square Punnett square. Example solves a two trait (two factor) test cross which can then be useful for solving a dihybrid cross on our handout here: http://www.amoebasisters.com/handouts.html This video uses vocabulary that was previously defined in the Amoeba Sisters Monohybrid Crosses video.

The Amoeba Sisters videos demystify science with humor and relevance. The videos center on Pinky's certification and experience in teaching biology at the high school level. For more information about The Amoeba Sisters, visit: http://www.amoebasisters.com/about-us.html

REFERENCE:
We cover the basics in biology concepts at the secondary level. If you are looking to discover more about biology and go into depth beyond these basics, our recommended reference is the FREE, peer reviewed, open source OpenStax biology textbook: https://openstax.org/details/books/biology

paragraphs: Occurs when neither allele on a particular gene can mask the presence of the other (i.e. there is no true “dominant” allele)

Upper and lowercase letters not used when representing incomplete dominance, rather two capitals letters.

paragraphs: In some varieties of flowering plants, petal colour is determined by two alleles which demonstrate incomplete dominance. One version of the allele, R1, encodes red flowers, while another version of the allele, R2, encodes white flowers.
c. Is it possible for the cross described in part b to produce offspring with white flowers? Explain.
No, it is not. The only way an offspring is white is if it is R2R2, which means both parents would have to have a copy of the R2 allele.

paragraphs: X-linked traits were discovered by Thomas Hunt Morgan through experiments with fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster).
He observed that white-eyed mutations appeared only in male flies when a red-eyed female was crossed with a white-eyed male.

Morgan proposed that the gene for eye color was on the X chromosome. Males (XY) inherit this trait directly from their mother, while females (XX) can carry the mutation without expressing it if they have one normal copy. This was the first evidence linking genes to specific chromosomes, shaping our understanding of sex-linked inheritance.

paragraphs: To have regular vision, a dominant allele must be present. So,
in females, two recessive alleles are required to be colour blind
In males, there is no second X-chromosome to carry a possible dominant allele; thus, only one recessive allele is required  be colour blind. This is why colour blindness is more common in males.

shapes.name: Google Shape;855;p73
paragraphs: To have regular vision, a dominant allele must be present. So,
in females, two recessive alleles are required to be colour blind
In males, there is no second X-chromosome to carry a possible dominant allele; thus, only one recessive allele is required  be colour blind. This is why colour blindness is more common in males.

paragraphs: A woman who is a carrier for color blindness and a man with normal vision have children.
What is the probability of their next…
child being a son who is color blind?

Alright..things are going to get a little confusing when working with sex-linked traits. First, we MUST use the chromosomes X and Y alongside the uppercase/lowercase letters to denote it is sex-linked and to calculate appropriate probability. Second, we must be careful with reading the question to know what it is looking for. Is it asking for a child, a son, an affected daughter, etc.?
Let XB represent the normal vision allele and Xb represent the recessive color blind allele. So our cross is:
0/2 = 0  (none of the daughters will be colorblind)
carrier: an organism that is heterozygous and ‘carries’ the recessive allele. You can not be a carrier for a dominant gene. You either have the condition or not in that case.

paragraphs: A woman who is color blind and a man with normal vision have children.
What is the probability of their next…
child being a son who is color blind?

Alright..things are going to get a little confusing when working with sex-linked traits. First, we MUST use the chromosomes X and Y alongside the uppercase/lowercase letters to denote it is sex-linked and to calculate appropriate probability. Second, we must be careful with reading the question to know what it is looking for. Is it asking for a child, a son, an affected daughter, etc.?
Let XB represent the normal vision allele and Xb represent the recessive color blind allele. So our cross is:
0/2 = 0  (none of the daughters will be colorblind)

paragraphs: Although females carry two X-chromosomes in each of their cells, only one of these chromosomes is active; the other one condensed into what is called a Barr Body.

The particular X chromosome that is inactivated in each cell is completely random. This mode of inheritance accounts for the colour patterns seen in tortoiseshell and calico cats. These are female cats that are heterozygous for the X-linked color traits. Each cell randomly inactivates an X chromosome and will express a random available color.  Therefore only female cats can have this random coloring pattern!

paragraphs: Note: We focused on examples on the X-chromosome (i.e. X-linked traits) mainly. There are Y-linked traits as well, but because only males have/need the Y-chromosome, there are a lot less genes on this and these are typically only relevant to male development and functioning. This is also why the Y-chromosome is much smaller than the X-chromosome.
So we often use sex-linked and X-linked interchangeable, because most sex-linked traits are X-linked.

shapes.description:
Explore how to solve Punnett squares that involve sex-linked traits, specifically focusing on X-linked traits. Video has a resource available here https://www.amoebasisters.com/handouts This 2023 UPDATED sex-linked traits Amoeba Sisters video has more detail and improved art from the old 2015 Punnett squares and sex-linked traits Amoeba Sisters video.
OLD VIDEO: https://youtu.be/h2xufrHWG3E
-----------
Table of Contents:
00:00 Intro
0:49 Sex Chromosomes
2:25 Solving Sex Linked Punnett Square Problem
5:40 Five Things to Keep in Mind
-------------
*TEXTBOOK REFERENCES*

Clark, Mary Ann, et al. “12.2 Characteristics and Traits - Biology 2e | OpenStax.” Openstax.org, 28 Mar. 2018, openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/12-2-characteristics-and-traits.

Urry, Lisa A, et al. Campbell Biology. 11th ed., New York, Ny, Pearson Education, Inc, 2017.

----------------------------------------
*ADDITIONAL DETAIL INFORMATION*
*More info on Hemophilia: https://www.cdc.gov/ncbddd/hemophilia/facts.html

*More about red-green colorblindness & other forms of colorblindness: https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/11604-color-blindness

*Biological sex described by NIH & Yale School of Medicine:
NIH: https://orwh.od.nih.gov/sex-gender
Yale School of Medicine:  https://medicine.yale.edu/news-article/what-do-we-mean-by-sex-and-gender/

*Footnote about "male" & "female" terminology from NIH at BOTTOM of https://orwh.od.nih.gov/sex-gender/sex-and-gender-in-health-and-disease

^^Above sources also explain difference of sex & gender. 

*This video is about traits on sex chromosomes. In most cases, females have XX chromosomes & males have XY chromosomes BUT as video mentions, this is not always the case.
Examples:
XXY: https://www.genome.gov/Genetic-Disorders/Klinefelter-Syndrome 
XYY: https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/47xyy-syndrome/
X: https://www.genome.gov/Genetic-Disorders/Turner-Syndrome
Info about SRY gene & also conditions related to variants in SRY gene:
https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/gene/sry/

----------------------------------------
*FURTHER EXPLORATION*
1. How did X and Y sex chromosomes get their names?
From Arizona State University's "Embryo Project Encyclopedia" https://embryo.asu.edu/pages/sex-determination-humans
 
2. Preeclampsia was mentioned as an example that many disorders may have a genetic component yet are NOT single gene traits (and thus can't be easily worked on a Punnett square). In addition, many disorders may involve autosomes and other external factors. As mentioned, the cause of preeclampsia is currently not well understood though gene involvement is being studied.

*Genetic Risk Factors: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamacardiology/fullarticle/2805948

*Recent News regarding Preeclampsia:
FDA clearance of Preeclampsia risk assessment assays: https://www.preeclampsia.org/the-news/research/thermo-fisher-scientific-gets-fda-clearance-for-preeclampsia-risk-assessment-assays

*Preeclampsia Foundation's Page of Research News: https://www.preeclampsia.org/the-news/research-news

3. Sex chromosomes in other animals can vary & may not be able to be worked in same type of Punnett square:

Sex chromosomes in birds? Written by a professor of genetics:
https://theconversation.com/how-birds-become-male-or-female-and-occasionally-both-112061

Platypus:
https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0405702101

paragraphs: Note: We focused on examples on the X-chromosome (i.e. X-linked traits) mainly. There are Y-linked traits as well, but because only males have/need the Y-chromosome, there are a lot less genes on this and these are typically only relevant to male development and functioning. This is also why the Y-chromosome is much smaller than the X-chromosome.
So we often use sex-linked and X-linked interchangeable, because most sex-linked traits are X-linked.

paragraphs: Often, more than two alleles may exist for a particular trait (i.e. although an organism only inherits two alleles for each gene, many different alleles can exist within the population)
In humans, for example, a single gene determines blood type. However, three different alleles exist:

Note: the gene is designated “I” or “i” depending on the presence of an antigen. IA thus indicates the presence of an A antigen on red blood cells, and IB indicates the presence of a B antigen. The absence of an antigen is marked by “i”

paragraphs: A woman with blood type B has a child with a man with blood type AB. The woman’s father had blood type O. What is the probability that their child is a son and has the blood type B?

Since the woman’s blood type is B, her genotype can be either IBIB or IBi. However, since we are told that her father has blood type O, his genotype must be ii and therefore must have passed on a i allele to his daughter. So the woman’s genotype must be IBi.

shapes.description:
For all of human history, we've been aware of heredity. Children look like their parents. But why? When Gregor Mendel pioneered the field of genetics, he began to try to answer that question, and now that we know about chromosomes, all of his work will make a lot of sense. Let's take a look at Mendel's work, his laws of segregation and independent assortment, and try to understand what these mean for genetics and inheritance.

Amoeba Sisters videos only cover concepts that Pinky is certified to teach, and they focus on her specialty: secondary life science. paragraphs: What must be the genotypes of individuals 2 & 3 of generation II? How do you know?
What is the most likely genotype of individual 3 of generation III? How do you know?
Rr and Rr → we know they must have at least a dominant copy as they are not affected. But they must also each have a recessive copy because they were able to produce affected offsprings.

It is most likely RR. Her partner, III-2 must be rr, and since none of their kids are affected this is likely because III-3 only has the dominant R allele. But technically, we can not be 100% certain since 4 kids is a relatively small sample size.

paragraphs: Extra: Genes and the Environment: Epigenetics
Recent findings have suggested that just because you possess a particular allele does not mean you will express it. This is due to epigenetics…
E.g. Breast cancer (people with the BRCA1 or BRCA2 allele are more likely to develop breast cancer, but only if something causes these genes to be turned “on”)

paragraphs: Typically, the inheritance of a particular trait is thought to follow Mendel’s law of independent assortment, allowing us to accurately predict the phenotypic and genotypic ratios of offspring. Occasionally, however, genes may be observed as “breaking” this rule…
Genes that are located close together on the same chromosome are called linked genes.
Alleles for these genes tend to segregate together during meiosis unless they are separated by crossing over.

Crossing over occurs when two homologous chromosomes exchange genetic material during meiosis I. The closer together two genes are on a chromosome, the less likely their alleles will be separated by crossing over

shapes.description:
We just learned about X-linked genes, but what about gene linkage in general? If two genes are on the same chromosome, we can say that they are linked. Are they always inherited together? Can the alleles rearrange in some way? Well don't forget about crossing over in meiosis! That complicates things a little bit. Let's check back with Morgan and his fruit flies to see how things panned out!

shapes.name: Google Shape;1257;p107
paragraphs: Genes that are located close together on the same chromosome are called linked genes.
Alleles for these genes tend to segregate together during meiosis unless they are separated by crossing over.

Crossing over occurs when two homologous chromosomes exchange genetic material during meiosis I. The closer together two genes are on a chromosome, the less likely their alleles will be separated by crossing over

paragraphs: Unlinked genes found on different chromosomes will assort independently and yield all possible allele combination in a 1:1:1:1 ratio.
Linked genes found on the same chromosomes will not assort independently and are only expected to yield the original/parental combinations:
Linked genes found on the same chromosomes will not assort independently, however crossing over may occur between then, yielding some recombinants
The farther apart the genes are, the greater the likelihood of crossing over and greater the number of recombinants.

paragraphs: Linkage Map for the Human X Chromosome. This linkage map shows the locations of several genes on the X chromosome. Some of the genes code for normal proteins. Others code for proteins that are associated with genetic disorders.
Which pair of genes would you expect to have a lower frequency of crossing over: the genes that code for hemophilia A and G6PD deficiency, or the genes that code for Protan and Xm?

Hemophilia A and G6PD would have a lower crossing over frequency because they are closer together. There’s a lower chance that the chiasma (break in the chromosome where crossing over occurs) will occur between these two genes.

paragraphs: Genes are more likely to be linked if they are found on the same chromosome
We know that two genes are linked if we see gametes with more parental genotypes than recombinant genotypes (because crossing over occurs less frequently when genes are on the same chromosome)
We also know that two genes are linked if we see a different ratio of parental & recombinant offspring than predicted

paragraphs: The relative distance between two genes on the same chromosome may be determined using a method known as gene mapping.
Recall that in non-linked (“normal”) genes, 50% of gametes will be parental, and 50% will be recombinant.
In linked genes, less than 50% of gametes will be recombinant due to reduced frequency of crossing over.
Genes that are closer together cross over less frequently. So, the lower the recombination frequency, the closer together they are.
For example, genes H and d will cross over less than genes B and H, producing fewer recombinant gametes.

paragraphs: The relative distance between two genes on the same chromosome may be determined using a method known as gene mapping.
Recall that in non-linked (“normal”) genes, 50% of gametes will be parental, and 50% will be recombinant.
In linked genes, less than 50% of gametes will be recombinant due to reduced frequency of crossing over.
Genes that are closer together cross over less frequently. So, the lower the recombination frequency, the closer together they are.
For example, genes H and d will cross over less than genes B and H, producing fewer recombinant gametes.

paragraphs: A map unit (mu), also known as a centiMorgan (cM), is a unit of measure for gene linkage. It describes how closely together are two gene loci (plural of locus) are located.

A cM is about 1 million base pairs long, but we don’t want to think of it in terms of an actual physical distance, but rather as a measure of the recombination frequency and therefore how close together those two genes are, relatively speaking.
For example, if hair colour and nose size are 25 map units apart, it means that 25% of the time they will cross over and create recombinants, as we have seen in this example
Named in honour of Thomas Morgan

paragraphs: A map unit (mu), also known as a centiMorgan (cM), is a unit of measure for gene linkage. It describes how closely together are two gene loci (plural of locus) are located.

A cM is about 1 million base pairs long, but we don’t want to think of it in terms of an actual physical distance, but rather as a measure of the recombination frequency and therefore how close together those two genes are, relatively speaking.
For example, if hair colour and nose size are 25 map units apart, it means that 25% of the time they will cross over and create recombinants, as we have seen in this example

Body colour, where black (B) is dominant to grey (b)
Wing size, where large wings (L) are dominant to vestigial (l)

Use a Punnett Square to represent the cross between a purple-eyed fly with vestigial wings and a fly that is heterozygous for both eye colour and wing size. List the predicted phenotypic ratio of this cross IF the traits for eye colour and wing size are not linked.
IF the traits are not linked, we can see in the Punnett square that the phenotypic ratio should be:
Red eyes	      red eyes      purple eyes	      purple eyes
Large wings	      vestigial w.   Large wings	vestigial w.

shapes.description:
In this video Paul Andersen explains how the frequency of recombination between linked genes can be used to determine the relative location of genes on a chromosome.  Thomas Hunt Morgan and Alfred Strutevant used the fruit fly to develop a theory of chromosomal inheritance and discover crossing over.

Do you speak another language?  Help me translate my videos:
http://www.bozemanscience.com/translations/

asset_recommendations.teaching_purpose: Genotype/phenotype reference for a simple X-linked recessive model
asset_recommendations.caveat: Adjacent Punnett tables still required; maintain allele meanings
Explain early cell-lineage inheritance and rare male exceptions; no diagnosis from photo
White patches have a separate genetic basis; cannot attribute all colours to X-inactivation
Do not ask students to diagnose genotype or disclose their colour vision
Does not show polygenic mechanism; do not infer ancestry/genotypes of depicted children
480px width; explain every used convention; do not substitute it for family-specific reading

asset_recommendations.teaching_purpose: High-resolution autosomal dominant pedigree for constrained genotypes
asset_recommendations.caveat: Global individual numbering 1-12 across generations; do not silently renumber

asset_recommendations.teaching_purpose: Autosomal recessive pedigree, unaffected partner remains RR or Rr
asset_recommendations.caveat: Transparent PNG needs suitable background; four unaffected offspring do not prove RR

asset_recommendations.teaching_purpose: X-linked recessive pedigree and obligate carrier deductions
asset_recommendations.caveat: No printed individual labels; identify people unambiguously; source slide80 cross typo must not be copied

asset_recommendations.teaching_purpose: X-linked dominant pedigree with affected father/unaffected mother comparison
asset_recommendations.caveat: Treat title as given model; does not prove model uniquely from a tiny family

asset_recommendations.teaching_purpose: Same X-linked dominant family at smaller size
asset_recommendations.caveat: Model given; printed numbering continuous

asset_recommendations.teaching_purpose: Same pedigree consistent with AD and AR
asset_recommendations.caveat: Do not identify a single mode as forced
Leftmost generation-II mother is forced carrier but image leaves second allele unknown
Answers visible; not an independent inference prompt
221x194 pixels; poor for full-width teaching
221x194 pixels; use exact label reading only if enlarged readable
221x207 pixels and answers already visible
215x235 pixels
271x186 pixels; title gives model
Apply only stated full-penetrance single-locus assumptions; small-family clues are not proof

asset_recommendations.teaching_purpose: Independent, linked without exchange, and linked with exchange panels
asset_recommendations.caveat: 396x450 pixels; original slide96 final text has wrong class ordering; diagram itself coherent
No allele loci labeled; pair with explicit phase/gamete table; only two non-sister chromatids exchange
Same-chromosome distant loci labeled Not Linked; needs statistical versus physical linkage qualification

asset_recommendations.teaching_purpose: Two homologues and relative B/H/d intervals
asset_recommendations.caveat: 269x282 pixels; keep B,H,d and b,h,D exactly; no numeric distances
Do not treat as a current clinical reference; labels are historical
Three repeated slides reference same asset; total16 is a small sample
Does not itself teach class identification
Map estimate, not physical scale or exact fraction of meiotic cells
Does not identify gene order by itself
Source provides only two distances; this is one possible order, not uniquely determined
Four duplicated tester rows can obscure fixed-gamete logic; source fictional model only
Associated source BRCA mechanism is wrong; photo adds no essential mechanism

verified_source_count_tables.caveat: phase assumed from source context; small sample not proof
third pairwise distance not supplied for unique three-locus order
